raw_case_text:
An eighteen-year-old student from one of the South Asian countries reported with a sudden blurring of vision and redness in the right eye (OD) for which he sought a local ophthalmologist's opinion. The patient underwent a lensectomy along with vitrectomy, elsewhere for suspected endophthalmitis. The vitreous sample was suggestive of fungal infection. He received intravitreal injection of Amphotericin B along with vancomycin and ceftazidime at the time of first surgery elsewhere. After the operation, he had perception of light. Two days after the surgery, a repeat intravitreal injection of Amphotericin B and antibiotics were administered, following which his vision did not improve. He was then referred to our institute, where on examination, he was found to have no light perception. The intraocular contents could not be seen because of anterior chamber being full of exudates. Ultrasound revealed the presence of total retinal detachment with shallow choroidal detachment.
Prior to the onset of ocular complication the patient had a history of diarrhoea for 10 days. The patient was advised evisceration of the right eye. At this point, the patient had fever touching up to 101 F, cold, cough, and vomiting. Once the fever subsided, the evisceration was performed under general anaesthesia. Following the evisceration, patient had intermittent fever with high Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels. The patient was tested negative for HIV. Clinical examination ruled out the presence of pulmonary tuberculosis.
A bacterial and fungal culture was put up for eviscerated material and the sample was subjected to direct examination using KOH/Calcofluor for fungus and Gram-s stain for bacteria. A few septate fungal filaments were seen in the KOH/Calcofluor stain, and a few Gram-negative bacilli along with pus cells were seen in the Gram-stained smear. The blood sample was processed for bacterial and fungal culture using the BACTEC (Becton, Dickinson and Company) system. Clean catch mid stream urine was subjected to conventional semiquantitative method of isolation bacteria.
After three days of incubation, Salmonella typhi was isolated from the eviscerated material and blood specimen, whereas the urine culture was negative for pyogenic bacteria. The isolated organism, from both the specimen, was subjected to a nested PCR amplification using primers targeted against the 16S rRNA gene following the protocol described by us earlier. The first round of PCR amplified products was then subjected to a DNA sequencing to find the sequence homology among the isolates. The sequenced data was analysed using the BLAST search tool and were aligned using the MultAlin software. The DNA sequences of organisms isolated from the blood and eviscerated material confirmed Salmonella typhi with 98% identity. The Multalin picture of 16SrRNA of the isolates was identical as shown in Figure 1. The DNA extracts of the isolates were also subjected to a RAPD (Bangalore Genei Pvt. Ltd) analysis to determine their clonal origin which showed that they belonged to the same clone as shown in Figures 2(a) and 2(b). The patient was treated with systemic antibiotics based on the sensitivity report.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old South Asian male student was referred for loss of light perception in the right eye following prior vitrectomy for sudden vision blurring and redness, preceded by a 10-day history of diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Prior to ocular symptom onset, the patient had a 10-day episode of diarrhea. He subsequently developed sudden blurring of vision and redness in the right eye (OD) and underwent lensectomy and vitrectomy at an outside facility for suspected fungal endophthalmitis, receiving intravitreal amphotericin B, vancomycin, and ceftazidime at surgery and again 2 days postoperatively. Because his vision failed to improve beyond initial light perception, he was referred to our institute. Around the time of planned right eye evisceration, he also experienced fever up to 101 °F, cold, cough, and vomiting, followed by intermittent postoperative fevers.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent lensectomy, vitrectomy, and two intravitreal injections (amphotericin B, vancomycin, ceftazidime) of the right eye at an outside hospital; student from a South Asian country.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right eye visual loss and redness, prior 10-day diarrhea, fever (up to 101 °F), cold, cough, and vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmologic examination of the right eye (OD) demonstrated no light perception (NLP) and an anterior chamber filled with exudates obscuring visualization of the posterior segment. Systemic clinical examination was negative for pulmonary tuberculosis, and temperature reached 101 °F preoperatively with intermittent fevers postoperatively.
objective.routine_investigations: B-scan ocular ultrasound of the right eye revealed total retinal detachment with shallow choroidal detachment. Postoperatively, serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was elevated. HIV testing was negative, and clean-catch midstream urine culture was negative for pyogenic bacteria.
objective.advanced_workup: Direct microscopy of eviscerated right intraocular tissue showed a few septate fungal filaments on KOH/Calcofluor stain and Gram-negative bacilli with pus cells on Gram stain. Culture of the eviscerated intraocular material and BACTEC blood culture both isolated Salmonella typhi after 3 days of incubation. Nested PCR amplification and 16S rRNA gene sequencing (BLAST/MultAlin) confirmed Salmonella typhi with 98% identity in both blood and intraocular isolates, and RAPD genotyping confirmed identical clonal origin.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Endogenous Salmonella typhi panophthalmitis/endophthalmitis of the right eye secondary to typhoid bacteremia (with fungal co-infection on microscopy), confirmed by isolation of clonally identical Salmonella typhi from both eviscerated intraocular tissue and blood cultures via BACTEC culture, 16S rRNA nested PCR/sequencing, and RAPD analysis. Pulmonary tuberculosis, HIV infection, and urinary tract infection were ruled out. Once acute preoperative fever subsided, the patient underwent right eye evisceration under general anesthesia and was treated with targeted systemic antibiotics guided by susceptibility testing.
